newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy turns to army to help fight Naples mobsters.
newsitem.headline: Italy turns to army to help fight Naples mobsters.

text.p: Italy plans to send troops to the crime-ridden southern city of Naples to help quell an upsurge of mob violence which has shocked the country.

Interior Minister Giorgio Napolitano announced the measure late on Sunday, but warned that the army alone could not defeat the Naples Mafia, known as the Camorra, which is locked in a bloody battle for supremacy.
"We will define within the week a provision for a limited and targeted use of the military in Naples," Napolitano told state television. "But this will not solve all the problems."
More than 80 people have been killed and dozens injured in an explosion of ruthless gang warfare which has swept over the Naples area since the start of the year.

Napolitano's decision came after another weekend of terror around the port city, which saw two suspected mobsters gunned down in broad daylight and a number of innocent bystanders, including an eight-year old girl, injured in the wild shootings.

"(The troops) will relieve some several hundred police officers in Naples who will then be able to deal directly in fighting the Camorra," the interior minister said in an interview with Corriere della Sera daily published on Monday.
Commentators speculated that around 600 troops would be drafted into the area to help restore law and order to a city which has been branded "the far west" by the Italian media.

Local hoteliers complained that the sight of armed soldiers on the streets might kill off a flourishing tourist boom in Naples, but many opposition politicians said the troop deployment should have come earlier.

"This is a bitter victory," said Alessandra Mussolini, granddaughter of World War Two dictator Benito Mussolino and a member of the rightist National Alliance. "We have been asking for the army for a year now," she added.
Some 40 Camorra clan operate in and around Naples and have a more fragmented organisation than the Mafia gangs which rule on the nearby island of Sicily.
Napolitano said recent police successes against the Naples mobsters had helped spark off the inter-gang battles as depleted clans struggled to gain dominance in the region.
"Unfortunately there is not an immediate remedy. There is no guarantee we can end this war between the clans," he said.

The constant stream of gang-related murders since the start of the year initially caused little stir in the Italian press, but the problem leapt to the public attention when a young woman walking home with her six-year-old son was killed by a stray bullet last month during a mob hit in central Naples.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi said his centre-left government would not flinch in the face of the Camorra.
"We cannot give an inch. We have to react without delay, and we will do this against the Camorra," he told Ansa newsagency at the weekend while on a trip to Spain.
It is not the first time Italy has decided to send troops onto the streets.

The army was called up in 1978 following the kidnap and murder of the then prime minister Aldo Moro and, in more recent times, soldiers were sent to the southern region of Calabria and the island of Sardinia to help combat crime waves.
Troops are still stationed in Sicily five years after they were called in following the murder of leading anti-mafia magistrate Paolo Borsellino.
